Platform-Capitalism on Steroids So i got recently unemployed, left my last company as they wanted me to leave. They offered me money to leave and as
they changed my working environment in an unpleasant way I decided to take the money. So now i find myself on the job market for IT specialists right in the middle of AI take-over. The jobs are shifting
towards AI automation or so. At least any code seems to be written now by AI, and in the best case reviewed by a human.
After thinking for a few days what job i am interested in, talking about it to AI, i start feeling over-helmed by the
requirements companies are asking for. Are there already Senior AI Architects in Germany? Not sure. Anyway, how do these changes concern me? Looking at the job market, everything is nowadays Frontend, DevOps, Finance or
Embedded it seems. Common Software Development vanished except for a few jobs at old-fashioned companies. I wonder who
is developing all those tools and libraries? This are spare time projects multi-trillion-dollar companies are built on.
Finally all application code is written either for iOS, Android or Web. Which eventually maps to Swift, Kotlin and
html5/css/Javascript. And Embedded is another field, hardware product development. Which I am just not motivated
anymore. So where to go from here now? What are the options? Finally dealing more with people, dealing more with what? Where to
head from here? Damn i lost traction in the market. Now spinning around myself. What is truly needed? Can this even be
determined as the market is changing so quickly? One things is definitely important. Build systems which not only build
but track, verify and release changes while still allowing quick rollbacks. Right? People want to deploy very quickly
new features to their customers while letting the customer test, but bugs are still possible, so rollbacks will be more
important than ever. Will they? The tricky will still be, while people using this new infrastructure, they feed AI with the solution training it
themselves to replace their works putting them into a situation where they need to try stay ahead of the machine's
skills. The faster they hustle the more they improve the machine, which does not need to breath. The better the machine
the more you hustle. It/IT looks to me like a mouse in a spinning wheel. Platform-Capitalism on Steroids.

Show HN: Move more with short random exercise challenges Background: I've been working on Sporadic for years, while software engineering has been my full-time job. That means this code is mine, and I know it well since it was built in the pre-AI era. However, AI has allowed me to expand the features to a place where I am more confident in sharing it. Why: As an engineer, I sit and look at a screen all day. My brother is a graphic designer and does the same. Our goal was to build an app to get us on our feet, and one where we could do it together. What makes Sporadic fun is a mix of short exercises at random times during your day that you can do with your friends. We've got stats, streaks, and community-wide daily challenges. The mix of social accountability, random timing of challenges, and a streak to hold onto make it an effective tool for convincing me to do some push-ups between meetings. How it works: Get a push notification to do a specific short exercise within a given time limit. These can also be done with friends, and you'll get a push when they complete one. A buddy doing the challenge is an incredible motivator. Tech: I started this project long ago to learn Swift and SwiftUI. The project is decidedly Apple, with a CloudKit database on the back end. One really cool thing this gives me is the ability to have an authenticated user based on their iCloud account only, so you don't have to create an account to use Sporadic and join up with friends. Otherwise, CloudKit is pretty frustrating to use, and it will make it more difficult to add support for Android. If there is any Android demand, please let me know! Conclusion: I've enjoyed using Sporadic myself and hope that someone else out there could benefit from it. I would love some feedback on what is good and what needs improved. Thanks for reading.

Show HN: Lettercamp – open-source static blog framework Hi HN, I’m Eric and I’m building Lettercamp, an open-source static blog framework. The repo is at https://github.com/lettercamp/lettercamp and the homepage is online at https://www.lettercamp.com . Writing good content has always been the #1 way that I’ve grown the reach of products I’ve worked on in the past. However, it’s always bothered me how many little things get in the way of writing and publishing high quality, first party content onto the web. Building a performant, SEO-optimized blog from scratch was always distracting from development on the actual product, and setting up a 3rd party CMS meant that my content always lived in someone else’s database. Storing content in a non-markdown format also made it difficult to draft and edit with the help of an AI agent. Lettercamp is a modern approach to creating a content site. It ships with all the little features you’d expect in a blog: pagination, authors, metadata, search, cross linking, related posts and more. It’s also statically built, which means that all your content lives in markdown in your codebase, so a deployed version is performant with no database to maintain. This means that you can focus on writing good content instead of vibe-coding a whole blog. I want to add more features to the framework over time, including better support for AI agents, built in localization, email sign ups, and more. The repo is released under the MIT license so that anyone can use the framework to create a content site. The goal isn’t to charge individual developers. The monetization path is to provide a cloud hosted version, that has an online editor that content teams can use. The main advantage of this is to decouple the blog from product deploys, so that teams can publish content without needing to push code. I would love to get your feedback on if this is a problem that might resonate with you or your team. I know that a lot of products create a /blog section at some point, and I wonder what solutions people are using today. My hope is that over time, Lettercamp can be the go-to solution for teams looking to set this up. Try it out: https://github.com/lettercamp/lettercamp and let me know what you think!

Show HN: Lynx – open-source fully-customizable AI workspace I was finding that managing multiple agent threads with walls of text was getting tiring and inefficient for me and that I wanted a more visual way to interact with my agents, so I built Lynx. Lynx lets you quickly build fully custom interfaces connected to your data sources (e.g. via MCP or API) and trigger agents running on your machine from them (e.g. with Claude Code or Codex). I built it as an experiment but have found myself doing 80-90% of my work from inside Lynx. I have my own Conductor-like workspace for coding, a Mail client, a workspace for my writing, and various others for dashboards and explorations. The best POI source you can think of is Google, but their terms are unfriendly and prices don't work for an indie dev. Other better priced options still do not let you store the POI data from their API in your own database. I was determined to have my own map view of all of the places people have reviewed, so I needed coordinates. The tech: My solution to this was a postgres database full of data I imported and filtered from OSM. This gives me full control over the data to with what I want. So now I have a really cool map view with pins that can scale to millions with no problem using pmtiles. The client side is built with React Native. This was just so I could easily launch on web and mobile. On web, RN has a hard time with SEO, so I had to display some raw HTML / CSS here and there. There are also plenty of challenges with bugs that would only appear on certain platforms, so keeping everything aligned was a constant game of whack-a-mole. Conclusion: I have a picture in my mind of a Sproutings map overflowing with places reviewed by parents, but the reality is that we have a chicken and egg problem. A platform that relies on user engagement to provide value isn't valuable until people have engaged. I quickly found out however that her PRs aren't visible via our methods, since most of her PRs are private/not on GitHub. I also wanted to create a place where people can easily see the amount of merges top accounts do each month, now that agents have the ability to create thousands of PRs themselves. Currently we only support public PRs as well as the contribution total that gets provided by GitHub directly: - A public PR only counts if it's public, merged, and authored by the account that's being looked up, and merged within the specified period. - I use GitHub's search API for PR counts. In a single GraphQL query we ask for 1 day per alias (is:pr is:merged is:public author:X merged:DATE), a whole month costs about 1 rate-limit point. Current limitations include: - People that merged their own PRs also count. - Agent workflows can increase a person's PR count by a lot. So a bot can generate thousands of small PRs. - Private work and pushes directly to main don't show as public PRs. Those profiles do, however, show up in GitHub's contribution count if they've activated private contributions on GitHub. I had to seed about 1,000 accounts at launch and anyone who's been looked up since is also tracked. We obviously cannot track every single account on GitHub. Claude Code's API billing depends on how often the cache expires Hello, HN! I’m Max, CTO at Hystax. We use Claude a lot in our development work, and we’re also trying to make coding agents cheaper to run. We built the open-source Kompressor for compressing identical tool outputs that agents constantly resend. In our Codex tests, we noticed a real cost reduction of 22.7%. But testing it with Claude Code, we found something completely different. In Claude Code, the cache plays a more crucial role than compression. Claude Code marks its messages with caching points. As a result, almost every request consists of a long cached prefix and a new, truncated final part. Based on practical experience with Opus 5.5, reading from the cache appears to cost $0.20 per million tokens, accounting for about 92–95% of the tokens charged for prompts. Meanwhile, a five-minute cache entry costs $5, which is 25 times more expensive than reading from the cache. When an agent needs to run a build or a longer training cycle, they face the problem of the cache expiring. The next request then has to write the prefix to the cache again. We saw this 33 times in a cycle of 89-task runs without compression. As a result, 927,000 tokens were rewritten, which is approximately one-third of the volume billed in full. Until now, we’ve deliberately left the Claude Code text uncompressed because overwriting any byte within a cached prefix would very likely cause it to become invalid. But here’s what we came up with instead: – Compress only the uncached part. On the first transmission, only the new part is compressed. Everything already cached stays byte-for-byte unchanged. Fragments shorter than 4,000 characters are sent in full, since compressing each fragment would be much more expensive than sending the entire dialogue as is. – Keep the cache active while the tools are running; don’t let it expire.
While the agent waits for a tool response (model building/training), Kompressor resends the last request every 4.5 minutes with max_tokens: 1, so Anthropic re-reads the cached dialogue, and the five-minute timer restarts. Pings stop on the agent’s next request, after ~50 min, on the first failed attempt, or if a ping finds nothing in the cache. – Switch to the one-hour cache only when necessary. 
After the first pause longer than 5 min, Kompressor requests a one-hour cache for that conversation. We ran Claude Code on the Opus 5.5 model through the Terminal-Bench 2.1 benchmark (89 tasks) and calculated the cost based on Anthropic's actual billing, including pings. The cost per run decreased from $35.35 to $28.30 (-20%). The percentage of tasks solved by the agent without compression was 89.9%, and 90.6% when using Kompressor. The number of tokens lost due to cache expiration decreased from 927,000 to 13,000. But there’s a caveat: the agent never solves the same task twice in exactly the same way, and the entire difference came down to just 4 out of the 89 tasks. We expect these savings to persist from run to run: about 11% from keeping the cache up to date, and a few more percentage points from compression. This effect is most noticeable on tasks where the agent waits a long time – more than five minutes – for a command to execute: model training, compilation, and long simulations. In those cases, costs decreased by 34%.
To try Kompressor, see the GitHub repo below. Setup is in the README. The default configuration already includes compression of new text only and a switch to an hourly cache on long pauses; “keep-warm” is off (the only request that the proxy sends on its own). To enable, add to your config: [proxy.providers.anthropic] 
     cache_keep_warm = true and then run: kompressor wrap claude The benchmark above was run with all these settings enabled. Here are cost calculations: https://optscale.ai/blog/claude-code-prompt-caching 
If you run long tasks in Claude Code, how often does the cache expire while a tool is still running? Have you seen this with other providers too?

Tell HN: I'm working on original approaches to tag-based file organization I'm creating a tool (starting with a TUI MVP) for exploring and managing user files with tags, breaking out of rigid hierarchical silos across devices. I'd love your feedback on how useful my approach could be to you. Here are the core features of my MVP, addressing typical concerns with tag-based/non-hierarchical approaches, like efficient discovery, the tedium of creating/managing tags, lock-in, and portability: - Query DSL: A simple but expressive query language is provided to search for files/folders, based on their tags stored in a local db. Tags can be bare or categorized, and the categories can be user-defined or system generated. - Dynamic Virtual Folders: Guided drill-down file browsing via query-backed dynamic virtual folders as a first-class feature. Research shows spatial browsing/exploration is just as critical to file discovery as direct search. - Heuristic auto-tagging & triage queue: Tags are automatically generated on initial indexing using sophisticated heuristics based on file/folder metadata (path, name, os metadata, etc). Any existing or newly created files/folders that remain under-tagged go into a triage queue for quick manual bulk or individual tagging. - Managed, flat, sharded storage: On import, files are moved, flattened and name-normalized with their tags, into a sharded internal store, with all subsequent access routed through the tool's interfaces. While this breaks from file managers that typically leave files in place, it enforces the workflow shift needed for non-hierarchical organization to work well. Tags can be exported back to standard folder structures at any time. - "Project" folders as atomic units: Project directories like code repositories are not flattened, and can be tagged and retrieved as single, atomic units (in addition to their contents), which avoids flooding listings with thousands of their nested files/folders. Portability & Privacy: All files and project folders retain their exact contents. Since their tags are embedded in their names, and the original structure can be exported back if desired, there is no lock-in or loss of tags if the tool and its metadata db are uninstalled. Also, although file paths and metadata might be sent to a central API server to support features like the automatic tags and dynamic virtual folders generation, file contents stay strictly local. Roadmap As mentioned, the initial MVP is a TUI which provides a rich interface for browsing, search, basic file operations, and import, plus a CLI for some basic administrative actions. Eventually, I plan to support:
- A native GUI interface
- Self-hosted and Cloud-hosted servers for web UI access
- Bring-Your-Own-Cloud-Storage (e.g., S3 and/or Google Drive) to replicate the internal flat shared storage in the cloud, for backup and access from other devices
- Import from IMAP, mobile devices, etc.
- Versioning What are your thoughts? Do you think these approaches address the limitations of hierarchical file organization, as well as the friction involved with typical tag-based tools? Would you be comfortable with file metadata being processed or stored in the cloud? And, do you think this tool could provide you enough value to pay for it?

Show HN: RealtimeVAD – trading false positives for 110ms earlier end-of-speech Recently I tried to hunt down latency bottlenecks in my local voice assistant. Looked at the waveform and saw Silero's probability lagging behind the actual end of speech I could see with my eyes easily. I thought there has to be a better way for my voice pipeline. Which does speculative work and cancels fast, so some false positives would not matter. So my idea was: once Silero says I'm in speech, what I need to detect is when the speech energy drops back to room noise level. Somehow algorithmically and as early as possible. Turned out a naive 10 ms energy check with a threshold tracking room noise does the trick. Combined with one simple rule: whichever says 'speech off' first wins, so it's never later than Silero. I lost my sense of engineering along with it. I was still the one accountable for software I didn't understand. The ability to regenerate the same piece of code multiple times and always get the same results in terms of functionality is called the deletion test and proves that your coding agent completely understands you. The idea is that every time part of the software needs to be changed, you regenerate a new version of the code based on the durable information you have about the system. You can repeat this process as many times as you want until you're happy with the change you're implementing. It's available at https://github.com/ebrake/pulumi-journaling Background: Pulumi recently detailed their journaling architecture ( https://www.pulumi.com/blog/journaling/ ), which changes how state snapshots are synced. Show HN: Armin – Modern Anki alternative with prerrequisite graphs okay, so a bit of context. back when i was studying at college, i was trying to optimize my learning process as much as possible, and i ended up discovering Anki and spaced-repetition as a concept. i ended up using Anki for quite a while and it did help me. i loved the concept... but i didn't like the app. it had me conflicted. on one hand, it allowed me to properly review the content from my classes (among other stuff), but on the other it had way too many quirks and complicated ways of handling things that i wasn't a fan of (in particular, the UX leaves a lot to be desired, although it has marginally improved in recent years). i ended up churning from Anki and just abandoning the practice of spaced repetition altogether. after some time, i ended up reading this article recommended by Justin Skycak https://lelouch.dev/blog/you-are-probably-not-dumb/ . 
the tldr is that knowledge has prerrequisites, and if you don't have them, you won't fully understand what you are trying to learn in the first place. and that was one of my annoyances with Anki. 
as i kept reviewing stuff (especially pre-made decks) Anki assumes all knowledge is in the same layer of understanding. it assumes that each flashcard is independent from the others, and that makes it difficult to actually progress while trying to learn a particular topic. 
Justin Skycak (the guy from Math Academy) ended up implementing spaced-repetition + prerrequisite graphs for math learning, and there i ended up seeing we could extend the concept more generally. one of the things Math Academy made me realize is that if we combine spaced-repetition (i.e. when we should review a card) with prerrequisite graphs (i.e. we keep unlocking new knowledge as we learn the prerrequisites), we can learn things more clearly and in a more structured way. that's where my "bet" goes. i want something like Anki, but with the option to create a graph of prerrequisites (e.g. you can't learn Y until you properly learn X). that's Armin. among other stuff, i also tried to fix some of the annoyances i had with Anki and make it as intuitive as possible to use. this is a non-exhaustive list of the things i worked on for this app: - UI polish of the interface. i tried to make it as intuitive as possible. - MCP server for letting agents read, edit and manage cards and decks. in particular, the MCP server is very useful for creating flashcards from any existing content you have. just point your agent to a resource (e.g. a pdf) and it will take its content and transform it into a deck with flashcards with its prerrequisites graph already created. - Anki-compatibility with caveats. the app supports bringing your existing Anki decks for most decks out there. however, some decks have custom cards that are not so easy to integrate seamlessly. there are plans to support custom cards in the future, but for now they are not implemented. - graph view that shows all your flashcards. in here, you can create a graph of prerrequisites and further structure your decks. - "concept cards". they work more like exercises. you provide the template of an exercise (e.g. how to calculate a derivative) and an agent creates variations of that same type of exercise while changing the details (like the values). we also have a paid plan for creating way more flashcards and use "concept" cards, but i built the free plan with generous limits so you can test the app without any issue. to be honest, i want the app to be as flexible as possible, and most people will probably only need the free plan. but hey, if you find it too tight, please hit me up and i'll see how i can improve the experience for everyone. the app is open source and MIT-licensed. you can find it here https://github.com/andy-spike/armin as for the rest, it is the same you would expect from a spaced-repetition flashcard app.

Show HN: Kapso – Iterative learning from enterprise data Hey HN! We're Alireza and Majid building Leeroo ( https://leeroo.com/ ). Previously we’ve built AI systems for products with millions of users, including at LinkedIn and Meta. We’re now focusing on building AI systems for enterprise data. Today, we're open-sourcing Kapso ( https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso ), an engine that runs experiments, deploys the best solution, and learns from every run. The nature of data work is iterative: investigate, form hypotheses, experiment, and improve based on what you learn. This bottom-up process is the only way to deliver meaningful outcomes quickly in large, messy enterprise data environments. Consultants gathering context in meetings or teams defining a business ontology upfront to fit into the data has no chance of execution, in quarters and sometimes years. An AI-native system should automate this process, compounding learning to each new investigation and implementation. For instance, one of our enterprise projects was moving a company off its old data estate onto a lakehouse with more than 30 source-system families, thousands of tables and transformations, and hundreds of BI reports. No individual or AI agent knew how that data estate was connected and operated. The only way to learn it was to investigate the company's repos, dbt models, documentation, and data itself and propose hypotheses about the estate, run experiments, and learn from them, until we understand how each system behaves and under which conditions. The iterative work goes beyond understanding how data and systems fit together, and the business operations. Building useful software is iterative too. Whether you’re optimizing a warehouse, building a lakehouse pipeline or predicting churn, you need to run experiments and learn what works best in that environment. As you deliver more projects, that know-how compounds, similar in principle to RL. RAGing documentation has little value until it has been tried in a specific environment and the consequences are learned. As with human engineering work, experimentation and learning should happen in a sandbox. We built Kapso for this kind of work, you give it an objective and success criteria, and it works towards an optimum solution that can be deployed on your stack. You can view a video walkthrough here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W4FHlza1fRs Here’s how it works… Kapso has a bank of lessons that are induced or deduced from the past experiments, and each carries a credence score, conditions on where it applies, and the evidence behind it.  For each new experiment, an ideation module proposes ideas considering the earlier lessons, re-ranks them by expected return against the budget each would use, and sends the top-ranked ones to the implementor. Because the bank keeps learning from the past experiments in that environment, the proposed ideas are better suited to it than generic hypotheses from an LLM or RAG. Also, results of each experiment are verified by a verifier module that no experiment can access and cheat. As we’ve found when building such systems, sometimes the success criteria and evaluation tests need to be evolved. The experimentation modules can propose updates to the metrics and criteria for the verifier to approve or reject. After each run, learn() updates the bank of lessons’ scores and boundaries using the evidence from that run. Changes to the bank can also be A/B tested by running otherwise identical builds with the previous and updated banks. The bank is built on git, so you can share your experience with others, list the banks available to you, and update them (`kapso experience share/list/update` in CLI). The system is model-agnostic and coding-agent-agnostic. kapso.deploy(solution, target_stack) follows the same workflow, runs a shorter experimentation loop to adapt the best solution to the target stack (e.g. Docker, Modal, BentoCloud, LangGraph). Every domain has a harness to start from, you can write your own domain harness with /kapso:harness in the plugin or through CLI (kapso harness new <name>), and compound over that by running experimentations. We ran it on some public benchmarks and live competitions, with the following results… - Predictive modelling on relational databases: first on RelBench, Kumo AI (now Nvidia) and Stanford's benchmark, ahead of the best tabular foundation model ( https://star-project.stanford.edu/relbench/leaderboard/ ). This shows that keeping the learning in the harness-level can beat foundational table models. Updating a bank of lessons costs far less than retraining a tabular foundation model. - ML Engineering: First on OpenAI's MLE-bench at submission, still among the top open-source systems ( https://github.com/openai/mle-bench/pull/107 ). - AI competitions: ahead of the best agent the ALE-Bench authors at Sakana AI reported, and running autonomously at the live International Olympiad in AI 2026, above all 471 human contestants and in the top three AI systems ( https://ioai-official.org/ai-models-track/ioai%c2%b2-2026-re... ). We have a public bank for ML and Data at Leeroopedia ( https://leeroopedia.com/ ): around 100k pages extracted by experimenting on papers and repos, about 6M requests a month, about 28% from AI agents. If you are at a growing company with a complex data estate across multiple systems and functions, and your data and AI team is stretched, we would love to help! https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso

Show HN: PharmA2A, an open protocol for pharmacy-to-supplier orders on A2A I am pharmacist, in France and I order directly from more than a hundred suppliers. Most orders are a web form, an email or a phone call . I built a buying agent for my pharmacy and the problem came fast: there is nobody to talk to on the other side. A supplier has a sales rep with a mailbox, sometimes an ERP. The idea is PharmA2A. It's based on the A2A protocol. PharmA2A says what they say. Five messages, each one a JSON Schema: supplier sheet, order , acknowledgement line by line, state of the shelf,  follow-up. Some rules are strict.  The order never has a pharmacy's price in it. Nothing is invented. And a message that says nothing is not a confirmation. One of the first answers we got from a sales rep was "looks good to me :)". Is that a confirmation? We had to decide. In the repo: the spec (CC0), a sample supplier agent  in about a hundred lines of Python, an email bridge for suppliers who only have a mailbox, and a demo pharmacy. It has carried real orders since October, in my own pharmacy. No supplier runs its own agent yet. I would like your opinion: is an A2A profile extension the right shape for this? And what would a supplier's IT team need to plug an ERP into it?
